title: Recurring decimals → fractions
examples: How do I turn 0.121212... into a fraction?
What is the difference between pure and mixed recurring decimals?
Can you show me the algebraic method with a different example?

explain.say: Today we learn to change repeating decimals into fractions. This process uses simple algebra. We will look at pure recurring decimals first. A pure recurring decimal has the repeating part starting right after the point.
Let us say the decimal is zero point three three three... We can write this as zero point three repeating. We assign this value to a letter, say x. So x equals zero point three three three...
Next, we multiply x by ten. Since only one digit repeats, we multiply by ten. This gives us ten times the original value. So ten x equals three point three three three...

Now we subtract the first equation from the second. Subtracting x from ten x cancels out the repeating part. This leaves us with ten x minus x equals three minus zero point three. So nine x equals three.

Finally, we solve for x by dividing both sides by nine. This gives us x equals three divided by nine. Simplifying this fraction gives us one third. So zero point three three three... equals one third.

faq.q: What is a pure recurring decimal?
faq.a: A pure recurring decimal is one where the repeating block starts immediately after the decimal point. For example, zero point seven seven seven... is pure.
asks: Where does the repeating part start?

faq.q: How do I handle a mixed recurring decimal?
faq.a: A mixed recurring decimal has non-repeating digits first, followed by the repeating block. We treat this by multiplying by a power of ten first.
asks: Does the method change for mixed decimals?

faq.q: Why did we multiply by ten in the first example?
faq.a: We multiplied by ten because only one digit was repeating. If two digits repeated, we would multiply by one hundred, which is ten squared.

faq.q: Does the number of digits repeating matter?
faq.a: Yes, the number of repeating digits determines the multiplier. If three digits repeat, you must multiply by one thousand, which is ten cubed.
asks: How many times do I multiply?
If it repeats three times, what do I use?

faq.q: Can I use this method for non-repeating decimals?
faq.a: No, this algebraic method only works for repeating or terminating decimals. If it stops, it is a simple fraction already.

facts: The decimal zero point six six six... is equal to the fraction two divided by three.
If two digits repeat, you multiply by one hundred to set up the algebra.
A terminating decimal, like zero point five, is already a simple fraction.
The algebraic method relies on subtracting the original value from a scaled version.

quiz.say: What fraction equals zero point eight eight eight...
quiz.why: When one digit repeats, you use the multiplier of ten, leading to nine times the value, which gives the correct fraction.

wrong.0: This mistake happens if you treat it like a terminating decimal and use the denominator 8.
wrong.1: This is incorrect because you used the wrong multiplier for the repeating pattern.
wrong.3: This is a common mistake because you only look at the first digit and divide by ten.

quiz.say: What fraction equals zero point twelve twelve twelve...?
quiz.why: Since two digits repeat, you multiply by one hundred, leading to ninety-nine times the value, giving the correct fraction.

wrong.0: This mistake ignores the fact that the pattern repeats infinitely.
wrong.1: This is wrong because you only used the multiplier for a single repeating digit.
wrong.2: This is incorrect because you did not account for the two digits in the repeating block.

quiz.say: What fraction equals zero point three five three five three five...? (Simplify your answer)
quiz.why: Two digits repeat, so we multiply by one hundred, giving ninety-nine times the value, which results in the correct fraction.

wrong.0: This is wrong because it treats the decimal as if it stopped after two places.
wrong.1: This mistake only considers the first digit and ignores the second repeating digit.
wrong.2: This is incorrect because the denominator should relate to the number of repeating digits.
